item.title: Sustainable Luxury Tourism: Opportunities, Tensions, and Impacts
item.content:encoded:
Kalliopi Chatzipanagiotou, University of Glasgow

Achilleas Boukis, University of Birmingham

George Christodoulides, American University of Sharjah

Raffaele Filieri, Audencia Business School

Luxury tourism is expected to grow faster than any other industry segment. Although scholarship on luxury tourism has expanded in recent years, much of this work focuses on its economic dimensions, often overlooking its broader sustainable, social and ethical implications. The relationship between sustainability and luxury tourism has received increasing attention in recent years, yet we know little about what sustainable luxury actually means, given the tension between exclusivity and responsible resource use. Furthermore, while many luxury tourists express concern for sustainability, there remains limited empirical evidence on how such concerns translate into actual decision-making or on the trade-offs they are willing to accept.

At the same time, the experiences of local communities and workers are largely overlooked, pointing to a broader gap around social inequality. Much of the discussion remains focused on minimizing environmental harm, with less attention given to how luxury tourism might actively support more regenerative and inclusive forms of sustainable development. Luxury tourism can amplify inequalities, concentrating wealth and privilege within exclusive enclaves while placing disproportionate burdens on local communities, ecosystems, and labour. These tensions between luxury value and impact raise critical questions about who benefits from luxury tourism, who is excluded, and how its growth reshapes societal dynamics, cultural authenticity, and environmental sustainability.

Technological innovation adds further complexity. Artificial intelligence, virtual and augmented reality, and other immersive tools are transforming how sustainable luxury is produced, mediated, and consumed. These technologies may democratize access and enhance personalization, yet they also raise concerns about authenticity, cultural representation, and digital exclusion. Additionally, there is a lack of robust methods for assessing the real environmental and social impacts of luxury tourism, while questions about the role of technology are only starting to surface, particularly concerning its environmental footprint and issues of access and inequality.

This Special Issue aims to advance knowledge and debate on sustainable luxury tourism by inviting research that explores how it is defined, experienced, and measured in today's global environment and across various contexts. We also encourage studies of emerging forms of luxury travel, including wellness, medical, and experiential travel, which bring to the fore new environmental concerns and tensions such as the commodification of care and inequalities in access to health and well-being. Research on sustainable luxury tourism, whether theoretical, conceptual, or empirical, is encouraged, particularly those that adopt holistic approaches and connect sustainable luxury theory with practical applications. Mixed-method and multi-method submissions are welcomed. Studies focusing on more than one country and culture, as well as those with a longitudinal approach, will be prioritised.

Potential topics

  • Designing and conceptualizing sustainable luxury tourism experiences
  • Luxury tourism consumption practices and sustainable behaviors
  • Emerging forms of luxury tourism through a sustainability lens
  • Cultural authenticity and heritage in sustainable luxury experiences
  • Personalization, exclusivity, and sustainability tensions in luxury tourism
  • Storytelling, experience design, and sustainability communication
  • The environmental and social dark sides of luxury tourism
  • Local communities, inclusion, and social value creation in sustainable luxury tourism
  • Labor practices and working conditions in sustainable luxury hospitality
  • Destination branding, image, and sustainable luxury positioning
  • Stakeholder collaboration and governance in sustainable luxury tourism
  • Sustainable luxury within tourism ecosystems and power dynamics

Timeline

  • November 1, 2026: Abstract deadline
  • May 31, 2027: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Just sustainability transitions in tourism
item.content:encoded:
Raymond Rastegar, Griffith University

Rami K. Isaac, Bethlehem University

Andrew Mzembe, Breda University of Applied Sciences

Lisa Ruhanen, The University of Queensland

The tourism sector stands at a critical crossroads. Amid accelerating climate crises, deepening socio-economic inequalities, biodiversity loss, enduring structural marginalisation, and regional conflicts, calls for systemic transformation have become increasingly pressing and unavoidable. While initiatives such as green transitions and the push toward net-zero have gained traction, driven by decarbonisation strategies, energy transitions, and technological innovations, these pathways are far from politically neutral. Transitions are not merely technical adjustments to energy systems or consumer behaviour; they are profoundly political processes that shape who benefits, who bears the burdens, and who has a voice or is silenced in the governance of change.

Sustainability transitions demand a critical interrogation of governance mechanisms, institutional lock-ins, market structures, and cultural imaginaries. Yet, approaches to transition within the tourism and hospitality sector often remain entrenched in technocratic and neoliberal logics that sideline questions of equity, power, and historical injustice. These omissions risk perpetuating and even exacerbating the very inequalities that sustainability agendas seek to address. A growing body of tourism and hospitality scholarship reveals that sustainability and justice are frequently treated as separate concerns. This disconnect presents a timely opportunity for scholars to advance integrated theoretical and empirical work that meaningfully connects sustainability transitions with justice-oriented perspectives.

Recent scholarship in tourism and climate policy underscores the growing relevance of Just Transitions, a concept rooted in environmental and labour movements and increasingly institutionalised by global organisations. In this Special Issue, we adopt the broader and more critical framework of Just Sustainability Transition (JST). This approach moves beyond narrow carbon and labour-focused agendas to interrogate fundamental questions: Who transitions? How do transitions unfold? What historical and place-specific factors shape them? For whom are these transitions imagined? And how does tourism contribute to or hinder wider sustainability transitions? These questions, often sidelined in dominant sustainability narratives, lie at the heart of the JST approach. JST foregrounds the reality that sustainability transitions in tourism are neither politically neutral nor uniformly experienced. They are embedded in structural inequalities, shaped by global power asymmetries, and conditioned by uneven capacities for participation, adaptation, and governance.

Despite the continued dominance of growth-oriented paradigms and market-led solutions in tourism which tend to obscure deeper questions of recognition, procedural, distributive justice, and restorative justice, emerging research across climate justice, regenerative tourism, multispecies ethics, and decolonial critique reveals the transformative potential of centring justice in tourism transitions. This Special Issue aims to advance critical debates by providing a platform for theoretical, conceptual, and empirical contributions that interrogate and reimagine transitions in tourism and hospitality through a justice lens. We particularly welcome work that draws on intersectional, decolonial, ecological, feminist, Indigenous, and multispecies justice perspectives to illuminate the tensions, trade-offs, and transformative potentials embedded in the sector's transition pathways. We also encourage submissions that conceptualise JST as a longitudinal and staged process, one that enables the identification and tracking of transitional justice markers across research, policy, and practice. This approach reframes sustainability not merely as a technical or managerial challenge, but as a profoundly normative and political project that demands inclusive, reflexive, and justice-oriented transformation.

Potential topics

  • Governance frameworks and institutional innovations for embedding justice in tourism transitions
  • Power, agency, and the role of private and public actors in driving (or resisting) transitions
  • Just sustainability transition imaginaries and realities across geographies: Global South and Global North perspectives
  • Intermediaries, social movements, labour unions and civil society in shaping justice-oriented transitions
  • Tourism workers' rights, precarity, and vulnerability in the context of transition
  • Climate change adaptation and mitigation through the lens of climate justice
  • Multispecies justice and posthuman perspectives in sustainable tourism
  • Gender justice and intersectionality in transition governance
  • Island and Indigenous tourism economies: toward self-determined transition pathways
  • Transition tourism: exploring new business models and regenerative alternatives
  • Methodologies for researching justice in sustainability transitions
  • Temporality and just transitions

Timeline

  • February 20, 2026: Abstract deadline
  • September 30, 2026: Manuscript deadline
